passages.t: Why do the wicked prosper? Racing with horses
passages.happening:
Jeremiah brings a case to God. ‘Righteous are You, O LORD, when I plead before You’ (verse 1). Yet he wants to argue: ‘Why does the way of the wicked prosper?’ (verse 1). Why do the faithless live at ease? God planted them and they took root and bore fruit. God is always on their lips but far from their hearts (verse 2). God knows Jeremiah's heart (verse 3). How long will the land mourn and the fields wither (verse 4)?

God answers with a question. ‘If you have raced with men on foot and they have worn you out, how can you compete with horses?’ (verse 5). If he stumbles in a peaceful land, what will he do in the thickets of the Jordan (verse 5)? Even his own brothers, his father's household, have betrayed him. ‘Do not trust them, though they speak well of you’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Jeremiah's opening is courtroom language. He grants that God is righteous, the judge who cannot lose a case, and then asks to argue with him anyway, using the word for bringing a legal complaint. Israel's faith gave room for this. Abraham argued with God over Sodom, Job demanded a hearing, and a psalmist asked why the wicked flourish.

The thickets of the Jordan were the dense jungle of tamarisk, willow and reeds along the river's lower course, home to wild animals, lions among them. God's question means: if you falter where it is safe, what will you do in the wild?

The chapter has no date. It fits the reign of Jehoiakim, when Jeremiah's life was often in danger. Verse 6 adds a bitter fact to the plot of chapter 11: his own family was against him.
passages.later: A psalmist felt the same: ‘For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked’ (Psalm 73:3). Habakkuk asked God the same kind of question: ‘Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?’ (Habakkuk 1:13).
passages.hard:
Why doesn't God answer Jeremiah's question about the prosperity of the wicked?

Many readers feel that verse 5 dodges the question. Jeremiah asked why, and God tells him things will get harder. There are several ways to read this. One is that God answers indirectly: verses 7 to 13 show that judgment is coming, so the wicked's ease is short. Another is that the Bible leaves the question open on purpose, as Job and Ecclesiastes do, and that God meets Jeremiah with his presence and a calling rather than a theory. A third notes that God treats Jeremiah as strong enough for a hard truth.

None of these makes the question go away, and the chapter does not pretend it does. Its gift is that the question is allowed, spoken by a prophet, and kept in Scripture.
passages.asks: God answered Jeremiah's question with a harder call. Ask what question you have brought to God that has not been answered as you wished. And ask whether you are being made ready for something harder than what tires you now.

passages.t: God forsakes his house, and a word for the neighbors
passages.happening:
Now God himself laments. ‘I have forsaken My house; I have abandoned My inheritance. I have given the love of My life into the hands of her enemies’ (verse 7). His inheritance has roared at him like a lion in the forest (verse 8). It is like a speckled bird of prey, with other birds circling against her (verse 9).

‘Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard; they have trampled My plot of ground’ (verse 10). The land is desolate, ‘but no man takes it to heart’ (verse 11). They sowed wheat and reaped thorns (verse 13).

Then a word about the evil neighbors who attack the land God gave Israel. He will uproot them from their land, and uproot Judah from among them (verse 14). ‘But after I have uprooted them, I will once again have compassion on them and return each one to his inheritance and to his land’ (verse 15). If they learn the ways of God's people and swear by the LORD's name, as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, they will be built up among God's people (verse 16). If not, God will uproot that nation (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
To call his people the love of his life is a startling thing for God to say for a people he is about to hand over. The judge grieves over the sentence.

The shepherds who trampled the vineyard are the foreign kings and armies who overran the land. Second Kings records that raiding bands from Babylon, Aram, Moab and Ammon were sent against Judah in Jehoiakim's last years. These are the evil neighbors of verse 14.

Verses 14 to 17 are surprising. The same nations that raided Judah are offered a future. If they learn to swear by the LORD's name, they will be built up among his people. The verbs of Jeremiah's call, to uproot and to build, now reach the nations.
passages.later: Second Kings records the raiders: ‘Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders’ (2 Kings 24:2). Isaiah also pictures foreigners joining God's people: ‘the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD’ (Isaiah 56:6).
passages.asks: God calls his own people the love of his life even as he hands them over. Ask what it means that God's judgment comes with grief, not coldness. And ask whether you can hope for a future even for those who have hurt you, as God offers it to Judah's neighbors.
